meta.title: Who really said "We have it in our power to begin the world over again"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Thomas Paine wrote it, in the Appendix to Common Sense (1776). A verified, correctly attributed line, later made famous again by Ronald Reagan.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We have it in our power to begin the world over again'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuinely Thomas Paine, from the Appendix to Common Sense (1776) — one of the rare feel-good revolutionary lines that checks out. Verified against the primary text.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1737–1809 · English-born political writer & pamphleteer of the American Revolution
answer.sourceLine: Paine wrote this in the Appendix to the third edition of Common Sense (1776). The wording is genuine and confirmed against the primary text — a rare case where a stirring, oft-quoted revolutionary line survives scrutiny intact.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Common Sense (Appendix to the Third Edition)

source.excerpt: Should an independency be brought about by the first of those means, we have every opportunity and every encouragement before us, to form the noblest, purest constitution on the face of the earth. We have it in our power to begin the world over again. A situation, similar to the present, hath not happened since the days of Noah until now. The birthday of a new world is at hand…
trail: The exact sentence appears in the Appendix to the Third Edition of Common Sense, between the lines on forming a constitution and “the days of Noah.”
The Online Library of Liberty quotes the same passage and dates it to Common Sense, 1776.
Wikiquote’s Thomas Paine page carries the sentence, though within its “Quotes about Paine” material rather than a sourced Common Sense entry.
source.excerptNote: The sentence stands as Paine’s own declaration, not a citation of anyone else; no earlier source for the exact line has been identified. The quotation marks often seen around it today are a modern editorial flourish — the original 1776 printing carries no such marks.

sourceLink.text: Read the Appendix to Common Sense at ushistory.org

source.rightsNote: Common Sense was first published in 1776, so the text — including this line from the Appendix — has long been in the public domain in the United States.

author.bio: Thomas Paine was an English-born political writer whose 1776 pamphlet Common Sense helped turn American opinion toward independence, selling in the hundreds of thousands. He went on to write The American Crisis and Rights of Man, becoming one of the Revolution’s most influential and most controversial voices.

misattribution.heading: Commonly re-credited
misattribution.intro: The line is correctly Paine’s, but it travels under other names because of a famous 20th-century echo.

items.why: Reagan quoted the line in his 1980 Republican National Convention acceptance speech and returned to it often, so many hear it as his — but he explicitly credited “Tom Paine.”

misattribution.truthLine: The words are genuinely Paine’s, from the Appendix to Common Sense (1776); later speakers merely borrowed them.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Paine wrote the Appendix as the American colonies teetered on the edge of open revolt. The sentence distills his whole argument: that independence was not merely a grievance to be redressed but a once-in-history chance to build a new kind of government from scratch.

The line has since become a shorthand for American optimism and reinvention, quoted by presidents and activists alike — most famously by Ronald Reagan, who used it to close his 1980 convention speech.
